doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: Church versus blues and gambling with crooked dice
summary: Griffin explains the church and blues coexisted, describes the hot clothes table, gambling, and being reported to his mother by Miss Ethel.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Was there any conflict between the church music and the religion and the secular blues that you were getting so fond of?

Oh yeah, yeah. They were — there wasn’t a strong conflict because — I’m going to tell this and then, you know in my neighborhood we had everything. When I say everything — on our street there was — three doors down there was people selling what we call hot clothes. You know, suits and everything, that people had shoplifted out of the stores and everything and, but deacons and, you know, all kinds of people would come there and they were religious people, you’d see them at church with that suit on and they got it from the hot table. Because it was almost a skill of survival. You know. But they weren’t frowning too hard on the blues, unless you had a parent that was really — don’t listen to this, this is the devil’s music and all that. Well me, I didn’t have it. I wasn’t confronted with that you know. People used to party and do whatever they had to do but you’d see them up in church every Sunday nodding. And I was a unique kind of guy. When I say unique I was borderlining on being a gangster — no, not a gangster but being a criminal or whatever. I had a group of my friends, we had a crooked dice little game going. So we would gamble and the guy would throw out the crooked dice to me and I’d win money. You know a lot of money. Now this I thought — I’m pretty sure my mother didn’t know about it and she probably didn’t and maybe could have. But one day one of her friends in the same place where they used to have the music and Miss Ethel was her best friend, you know, my mother’s friend. And Miss Ethel would come and get me and take me to the cafe and I would dance and do all kinds of stuff and she would give me maybe a little sip of beer or something. My mother didn’t know about that. My mother was real strict, you know, a Christian person. But Miss Ethel would take me out and I could dance and she maybe’d give me a little sip of beer or stuff. So but Miss Ethel told my mother, “My name is James Richard,” she said, “Ruby James Richard is down there. He’d be gambling with the guys.” Now I was trying to be very slick and I probably thought I was real slick. I knew the time my mother would come because I had to keep my sisters, you know and everything, feed them and everything, wash the dishes and everything. So I would race home and be home and everything is clean and clear and everything, and be right there, and I always would make sure that I would be on time. So one day I was in my fifties.
